questions.q: Hammurabi, known for a famous code of laws, was a king of
questions.explanation: Hammurabi ruled Babylon in Mesopotamia.

questions.q: The early use of the wheel and of cuneiform writing is associated with which civilisation?
questions.explanation: The Sumerians of southern Mesopotamia developed cuneiform and used wheeled vehicles early.

questions.q: Cuneiform signs were made by pressing a reed stylus into
questions.explanation: Mesopotamian scribes wrote on wet clay tablets.

questions.q: Why did ancient Egyptians practise mummification?
options: They believed in life after death and wanted to preserve the body
It was a way of making cloth
questions.explanation: Preserving the body was linked to beliefs about the afterlife.

questions.q: A ruler's laws carved on a stone pillar and displayed for people to see suggest that
options: the ruler tried to apply written, publicly known laws across the kingdom
questions.explanation: Publicly displayed laws point to an attempt at uniform, known rules.

questions.q: Why did Sumerian city-states need record keeping?
options: Managing grain stores, trade and taxes required accurate records, which encouraged writing
questions.explanation: The needs of administration and trade helped writing to develop.

questions.q: What were ziggurats?
questions.answer: Ziggurats were large stepped temple towers built in Mesopotamian cities, dedicated to the city's god. They were also centres of religious and economic life.
questions.explanation: They show the importance of religion in early city life.

questions.q: Explain how the use of iron changed farming and warfare.
questions.answer: Iron was harder and cheaper than bronze, so iron ploughs and tools made it easier to clear land and increase crop production. Iron weapons were stronger and more widely available, which changed warfare.
keyPoints: better ploughs and tools raised production
questions.explanation: Iron technology spread widely because ore was more common than the metals for bronze.

questions.q: The Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople in the year
questions.explanation: Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453.

questions.q: William of Normandy won the Battle of Hastings in the year
questions.explanation: The Norman conquest of England began with Hastings in 1066.

questions.q: Charlemagne was crowned Emperor in 800 CE by the
questions.explanation: Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne in Rome.

questions.q: In medieval Europe, knights were
options: mounted warriors who served a lord
questions.explanation: Knights fought on horseback in return for land or protection.

questions.q: Monasteries in medieval Europe helped to preserve learning because
questions.explanation: Before printing, monks copied and kept many ancient and religious texts.

questions.q: The Black Death of the fourteenth century affected European feudal society because
options: the death of many workers made labour scarce and gave peasants more bargaining power
it ended all trade for ever
questions.explanation: With fewer workers, labourers could demand better terms.

questions.q: Describe the role of the Church in medieval Europe.
questions.answer: The Church was the main religious authority and also owned land and ran schools and monasteries. It influenced the lives of people and the decisions of rulers.
keyPoints: owned land, ran schools and monasteries
questions.explanation: The Church was one of the most powerful institutions of the period.

questions.q: Compare the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire in two respects.
questions.answer: In the Republic, power was shared among elected magistrates and the Senate, while in the Empire the emperor held supreme power. The Republic was mainly centred on the city and its neighbourhood, whereas the Empire ruled a far larger territory.
questions.explanation: The Republic gave way to rule by an emperor from the time of Augustus.

questions.q: Which English scientist is associated with the theory of evolution by natural selection?
questions.explanation: Charles Darwin proposed evolution by natural selection.

questions.q: The Renaissance in Europe is generally dated to roughly which period?
questions.explanation: The Renaissance began in the fourteenth century in Italy and spread over the next centuries.

questions.q: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome?
questions.explanation: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in the early sixteenth century.

questions.q: The 'spinning jenny' was invented to speed up the making of
questions.explanation: The spinning jenny allowed several threads to be spun at once.

questions.q: The Reformation weakened the religious unity of Western Europe because
options: new Protestant churches broke away from the Pope's authority
questions.explanation: Protestant churches formed independently of Rome, ending the single Western Church.

questions.q: Which was a long-term effect of the American and French Revolutions?
options: They ended all monarchies at once
They stopped the growth of nationalism
They spread ideas of popular sovereignty and rights that inspired later movements
questions.explanation: Their ideas influenced reform and independence movements in many places.

questions.q: What is meant by humanism in the Renaissance?
questions.answer: Humanism was an outlook that gave importance to human beings, their abilities and worldly life, and encouraged the study of classical Greek and Roman writings. It led to new interest in art, literature and science.
keyPoints: importance of human beings and worldly life
new interest in arts and sciences
questions.explanation: It was the central intellectual movement of the Renaissance.

questions.q: Explain how the Scientific Revolution changed the way people understood the world.
questions.answer: Thinkers such as Copernicus, Galileo and Newton relied on observation, experiment and mathematics rather than only on old authorities. They showed that nature follows laws which can be discovered, which changed ideas about the universe.
questions.explanation: It established the scientific method as a way of gaining knowledge.

questions.q: Which of these is a sedimentary rock?
questions.explanation: Sandstone forms from compacted sand grains.

questions.q: A mountain through which lava erupts is called a
questions.explanation: A volcano is an opening through which lava, ash and gases are ejected.

questions.q: The 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific Ocean is known for
questions.explanation: Many plate boundaries around the Pacific cause many earthquakes and volcanoes.

questions.q: A flat-topped, elevated area of land is called a
questions.explanation: A plateau is raised land with a relatively flat top.

questions.q: Mid-ocean ridges form where plates
options: move apart and new crust forms from rising magma
questions.explanation: At diverging boundaries magma rises and creates new oceanic crust.

questions.q: Why are deep ocean trenches found near zones where plates converge?
options: One plate sinks beneath another, creating a deep trench
questions.explanation: Subduction pulls the sinking plate down, forming a trench.

questions.q: Name any two types of mountains and give an example of each.
questions.answer: Fold mountains, such as the Himalayas or the Alps, are formed by compression of rock layers. Volcanic mountains, such as Mount Fuji, are built by erupted lava and ash.
questions.explanation: Mountains are classified by the way they were formed.

questions.q: Describe how the work of a river changes from its upper course to its lower course.
questions.answer: In the upper course the river flows fast on steep slopes and mainly erodes, cutting deep V-shaped valleys. In the lower course the slope is gentle and the river deposits sediments, forming floodplains and deltas.
questions.explanation: Slope and speed of flow determine whether a river erodes or deposits.

questions.q: The Earth completes one rotation on its axis in about
questions.explanation: One rotation takes about 24 hours and causes day and night.

questions.q: Which gas in the air is used by living beings for breathing?
questions.explanation: Most organisms need oxygen for respiration.

questions.q: Because of the Earth's rotation, winds in the Northern Hemisphere are deflected to the
questions.explanation: The Coriolis effect turns winds to the right in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: The imaginary lines that run from the North Pole to the South Pole are called
questions.explanation: Lines of longitude, or meridians, join the poles.

questions.q: On which date does the Sun shine vertically over the Tropic of Cancer?
questions.explanation: The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer at the June solstice.

questions.q: Why do hot deserts often show a large difference between day and night temperatures?
options: Clear, dry air lets heat escape quickly after sunset
questions.explanation: With little cloud or moisture, the ground loses heat rapidly at night.

questions.q: Differentiate between evaporation and condensation.
questions.answer: Evaporation is the change of liquid water into water vapour, usually by heat. Condensation is the change of water vapour back into liquid droplets when air cools.
questions.explanation: Both are steps of the water cycle.

questions.q: Explain how burning fossil fuels can strengthen the greenhouse effect.
questions.answer: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas. More greenhouse gases in the air trap more heat, which can raise the average temperature of the Earth.
questions.explanation: Rising greenhouse gas levels intensify the natural greenhouse effect.

questions.q: Which of these is a fossil fuel?
questions.explanation: Coal formed from the remains of ancient plants.

questions.q: A habitat is
options: the natural home of an organism
questions.explanation: A habitat is where an organism normally lives.

questions.q: Which kind of forest sheds its leaves in the dry season?
questions.explanation: Monsoon forests shed leaves in the dry season to reduce water loss.

questions.q: Tundra vegetation consists mainly of
questions.explanation: The cold polar climate supports only mosses, lichens and small plants.

questions.q: Planting trees on bare land helps by
options: absorbing carbon dioxide, binding soil and providing habitat
questions.explanation: Trees take in carbon dioxide, hold the soil and shelter animals.

questions.q: Coral reefs are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea because they
options: support a very large variety of marine life
questions.explanation: Reefs shelter a great diversity of species, like rainforests on land.

questions.q: What is a biosphere reserve?
questions.answer: A biosphere reserve is a protected area set aside to conserve the plants, animals and microbes of an ecosystem along with the traditional ways of life of people living there.
questions.explanation: Biosphere reserves aim to protect nature while allowing sustainable use.

questions.q: Soil is renewable but forms very slowly. What does this imply for its use?
questions.answer: Soil takes hundreds or thousands of years to form, so soil lost by erosion cannot be quickly replaced. It must be protected by measures such as terracing, afforestation and avoiding overgrazing.
questions.explanation: Slow formation makes careful use of soil essential.

questions.q: Peninsular India is bordered on the east by the
questions.explanation: The Bay of Bengal lies along the east coast.

questions.q: The Standard Meridian of India is approximately at
questions.explanation: Indian Standard Time is based on 82°30′ E.

questions.q: The Andaman and Nicobar Islands lie in the
questions.explanation: These islands lie in the Bay of Bengal.

questions.q: The Lakshadweep Islands are mostly
questions.explanation: The Lakshadweep group consists of coral atolls.

questions.q: The Indo-Gangetic plains support a dense population mainly because
options: fertile soil, water and flat land favour agriculture and settlement
questions.explanation: Fertile alluvium, rivers and level land support intensive farming and large populations.

questions.q: The Western Ghats' windward slopes have dense evergreen forests because
options: the southwest monsoon causes heavy orographic rain
questions.explanation: Moist monsoon winds are forced up the slopes, giving heavy rainfall.

questions.q: Name any four major soil types found in India.
questions.answer: Alluvial soil, black soil, red soil, laterite soil and desert (arid) soil are among the major types.
questions.explanation: Soil types in India are related to rock, climate and relief.

questions.q: Why is the climate of India described as monsoon type even though there are large regional variations?
questions.answer: The seasonal reversal of winds and the arrival of the southwest monsoon rain shape the rhythm of the year across most of the country. Regional differences in temperature and rainfall occur within this common pattern.
keyPoints: monsoon rain dominates the annual cycle
questions.explanation: The monsoon is the unifying element of Indian climate.

questions.q: The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution of India on
questions.explanation: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: India is described as a 'Union of States' in which Article?
questions.explanation: Article 1 says that India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.

questions.q: Which of these is a Directive Principle of State Policy?
options: Equal pay for equal work for men and women
questions.explanation: Equal pay for equal work is a Directive Principle.

questions.q: The Constitution of India provides for
options: single citizenship for the whole country
questions.explanation: India has a single citizenship common to the whole country.

questions.q: The Constitution divides powers between the Union and States but gives the Centre special strength in some situations. This arrangement is best described as
options: a federation with a strong Centre
questions.explanation: India is a federal system with a tilt towards the Centre.

questions.q: Why did the framers make the Fundamental Rights enforceable by courts?
options: So that rights stay as advice only
So that rights are protected even against encroachment by the government
To reduce the role of courts
questions.explanation: Court enforcement gives citizens a remedy against violations, including by the State.

questions.q: What was the Constituent Assembly of India and what task did it perform?
questions.answer: The Constituent Assembly was a body of representatives that met from 1946 to draft the Constitution of India. It debated and adopted the Constitution in 1949.
questions.explanation: The Assembly's work produced the Constitution that came into force in 1950.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'basic structure' of the Constitution?
questions.answer: The Supreme Court held in the Kesavananda Bharati case of 1973 that Parliament can amend the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure. Features such as democracy and judicial review are seen as part of it.
questions.explanation: The doctrine limits Parliament's power to amend the Constitution.

questions.q: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of
options: religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
questions.explanation: Article 15 forbids discrimination on those grounds.

questions.q: Which Article guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment?
questions.explanation: Article 16 deals with equality of opportunity in public employment.

questions.q: Which writ is issued to stop a lower court from acting beyond its jurisdiction?
questions.explanation: A writ of prohibition forbids a lower court from exceeding its authority.

questions.q: Under which Article can High Courts issue writs?
questions.explanation: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs.

questions.q: A student says her right to freedom of expression allows her to abuse a classmate in public. What is the correct response?
options: Freedom of expression is subject to reasonable restrictions and does not allow harming others' dignity
questions.explanation: Rights come with reasonable limits so that others' rights are protected.

questions.q: Why is the Right to Information considered useful in a democracy?
options: It helps citizens hold public authorities accountable
questions.explanation: Access to information lets citizens check the work of public bodies.

questions.q: State two differences between the rights of a citizen and those of a foreigner in India.
questions.answer: Citizens can vote and contest elections and hold some high public offices, which foreigners cannot. Some Fundamental Rights, such as those in Articles 15, 16 and 19, are available only to citizens, while rights such as Article 21 are available to all persons.
keyPoints: citizens can vote and hold certain offices
some Fundamental Rights only for citizens
questions.explanation: Citizenship carries additional political rights.

questions.q: How does the idea of secularism help in a society with many religions?
questions.answer: A secular State does not favour any religion, so followers of all faiths have equal rights and can practise their beliefs freely. This helps maintain peace and equal citizenship in a diverse society.
keyPoints: State does not favour any religion
equal rights and freedom to practise
questions.explanation: Secularism protects both religious freedom and equality.

questions.q: Who heads the real executive in a State government?
questions.explanation: The Chief Minister, with the State Council of Ministers, exercises real executive power.

questions.q: Elections to the Lok Sabha are held on the basis of
questions.explanation: Every adult citizen has one vote under universal adult franchise.

questions.q: Judges of the Supreme Court are formally appointed by the
questions.explanation: The President appoints them after consultation, as laid down by the Constitution.

questions.q: A no-confidence motion tests whether the government
options: still has the support of the majority in the Lok Sabha
questions.explanation: If the motion is passed, the government must resign.

questions.q: Why is it important to keep the judiciary separate from the executive?
options: Judges can decide cases impartially without pressure from the government
Ministers should choose judges at will
questions.explanation: Independence allows courts to give fair judgments, even against the government.

questions.q: Why does India's Parliament have two Houses?
options: To represent the people directly and also the States, allowing review of legislation
questions.explanation: The Lok Sabha represents the people and the Rajya Sabha represents the States, and it provides a second review of laws.

questions.q: Mention two functions of the Chief Minister of a State.
questions.answer: The Chief Minister heads the State Council of Ministers and leads the State government's policy. The Chief Minister also advises the Governor and allocates portfolios among ministers.
questions.explanation: The Chief Minister is the real head of the State executive.

questions.q: What is Public Interest Litigation (PIL), and why is it useful?
questions.answer: PIL allows any person or group to approach a court for the protection of the public interest or the rights of people who cannot easily approach it themselves. It makes justice more accessible to the poor and disadvantaged.
keyPoints: anyone may approach court on public issues
helps those who cannot approach court
questions.explanation: PIL widened the role of courts in protecting public interests.

questions.topic: Political Concepts: Freedom, Equality and Justice
questions.q: Who wrote the book 'The Social Contract'?
questions.explanation: Rousseau wrote The Social Contract in 1762.

questions.topic: Political Concepts: Freedom, Equality and Justice
questions.q: Treating everyone alike under the law, with no special privileges, is called
questions.explanation: Equality before law means that the law applies equally to all.

questions.topic: Political Concepts: Freedom, Equality and Justice
questions.q: A right that belongs to every person simply because they are human is called a
questions.explanation: Human rights belong to all persons by virtue of being human.

questions.topic: Political Concepts: Freedom, Equality and Justice
questions.q: In politics, the word 'minority' usually refers to a group that is
options: smaller in number than the rest of the population and often with a distinct identity
questions.explanation: Minorities are groups that are fewer in number than the rest and often share a distinct identity.

questions.topic: Political Concepts: Freedom, Equality and Justice
questions.q: Why is the rule of law essential for protecting liberty?
options: It lets rulers act as they please
It ensures those in power are also bound by law and cannot act arbitrarily
It allows laws to change daily
questions.explanation: When even rulers must follow the law, citizens are secure against arbitrary action.

questions.topic: Political Concepts: Freedom, Equality and Justice
questions.q: Which situation best shows a lack of procedural justice?
options: Both sides are heard before a decision
A person is punished without being allowed to present their side
questions.explanation: Fair procedure requires a hearing for the person affected.

questions.topic: Political Concepts: Freedom, Equality and Justice
questions.q: Name and briefly explain the main kinds of equality.
questions.answer: Political equality gives all citizens equal rights such as the vote. Social equality means equal status and dignity, without discrimination. Economic equality concerns reducing large gaps in wealth and income.
questions.explanation: Different kinds of equality relate to politics, society and the economy.

questions.topic: Political Concepts: Freedom, Equality and Justice
questions.q: Why does a fair procedure matter for justice?
questions.answer: Even a correct outcome may seem unjust if the process was biased or secret. A fair hearing, equal treatment and reasons for decisions build trust and reduce the chance of error or abuse.
questions.explanation: Justice depends on how decisions are reached as well as on the results.

questions.q: Which type of economic system did India adopt after independence?
questions.explanation: India adopted a mixed economy with public and private sectors.

questions.q: The Green Revolution began in India in the
questions.explanation: High-yielding varieties were introduced in the mid-to-late 1960s.

questions.q: In economics, 'globalisation' refers to
options: greater integration of economies through trade, investment and technology flows
questions.explanation: Globalisation means growing linkages among national economies.

questions.q: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) was established in the year
questions.explanation: The WTO was set up in 1995.

questions.q: Why was agriculture given priority in the First Five Year Plan?
options: Because of food shortages after independence and the need to raise output
questions.explanation: The economy was largely agricultural and food supply was a pressing concern.

questions.q: Opening the economy to imports can affect a domestic producer by
options: bringing greater competition, which may push for improvement or cause losses
questions.explanation: Competition from imports can raise efficiency but hurt weak firms.

questions.q: What is meant by the poverty line?
questions.answer: The poverty line is a minimum level of income or consumption expenditure, set to buy a basic standard of food and other necessities. People below it are counted as poor.
keyPoints: minimum level of income or expenditure
questions.explanation: It is used to measure the extent of poverty.

questions.q: Explain why the Green Revolution had unequal regional effects.
questions.answer: It worked best in areas with assured irrigation and good infrastructure, such as Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, and mainly for wheat and rice. Regions without irrigation and farmers with small holdings gained less.
keyPoints: less gain for unirrigated areas and small farmers
questions.explanation: The new technology needed water, inputs and credit.

questions.q: A study that collects information from every household in a village uses the method of
questions.explanation: Covering every unit of the population is a census.

questions.q: A questionnaire is a tool used for
questions.explanation: A questionnaire is a set of questions for collecting data.

questions.q: The arithmetic mean of 2, 3, 3, 4 and 8 is
questions.explanation: The sum is 20, and 20 divided by 5 is 4.

questions.q: The mode of the data 2, 3, 3, 4 and 8 is
questions.explanation: The value 3 occurs most often.

questions.q: A price index in the base year is 100. If the index this year is 125, prices have
options: risen by 25 per cent compared with the base year
questions.explanation: An index of 125 means a 25 per cent rise over the base year.

questions.q: In a country where a few people are extremely rich, the mean income may
options: be lower than what most people earn
overstate what a typical person earns
questions.explanation: A few very high incomes pull the mean above the typical income.

questions.q: What is the difference between a population and a sample?
questions.answer: A population is the entire group about which information is wanted. A sample is a smaller part of that group chosen to represent it.
questions.explanation: Samples are used to learn about a population without studying every unit.

questions.q: Why should a researcher be careful when using secondary data?
questions.answer: Secondary data were collected by others for a different purpose, so definitions may differ, they may be outdated or contain errors. The researcher should check the source and its reliability.
questions.explanation: Data quality affects the reliability of conclusions.
